h1: Investor Renovation Contractor in Baton Rouge
intro: In Baton Rouge, the most important line on a rehab scope is often a date: August 2016. The flood that month put water into tens of thousands of homes across the parish and next door in Livingston Parish, many of them outside the high-risk flood zones where nobody expected it. Some were gutted and rebuilt well, some were patched, and some still carry the damage behind fresh paint. Knowing which kind of house you are buying is step one. Genstone Construction works with Baton Rouge investors on fix-and-flip, BRRRR, single-family rental, small multifamily, FHA 203(k) and REO projects, coordinating vetted, licensed local contractors while a designated field manager runs each job. The free Pre-Offer Rehab Review checks flood history, foundation, roof and systems against your ARV before you commit. You then get a detailed scope with a draw schedule, City-Parish permits handled, remote progress documentation and no upfront payment.
housingStock:
Baton Rouge's housing is younger than New Orleans' and more spread out, with a few older cores and a lot of mid-century growth. The oldest investable houses are downtown in Spanish Town and Beauregard Town, which hold nineteenth- and early twentieth-century cottages and shotgun-style houses on piers, many inside designated historic districts. Just east and south, the Garden District, Mid City, Capital Heights and Southdowns developed through the 1920s, 1930s and 1940s with Craftsman bungalows, Tudor Revival cottages and modest frame and brick houses, a mix of raised pier foundations and early slabs. Old South Baton Rouge, between downtown and LSU, has older cottages and shotgun houses, some well kept and some long neglected.

After World War II the city spread east and south. Bernard Terrace, Broadmoor, Sherwood Forest, Tara and many surrounding subdivisions are dominated by brick ranch houses from the 1950s through the 1970s, almost all on slab foundations. Those houses are the core of the investor market: three bedrooms, simple roof lines, and systems that are now well past original life. Expect galvanized supply lines in the earliest ranches, cast-iron drains under the slab, older electrical panels, and ductwork in attics that bake through the summer.

Two regional factors cut across eras. The first is water. The 2016 flood hit houses in many of these neighborhoods and in suburbs like Central, Denham Springs and Zachary, and repairs ranged from complete gut rehabs to quick cosmetic covers. The second is the ground. Clay soils shrink and swell with the seasons, and a known geologic fault system crosses the parish, so slab cracking and pier movement are common inspection findings. Lead paint is likely in anything built before 1978, and mid-century materials can contain asbestos.

commonIssues.title: Hidden 2016 flood damage
commonIssues.body: Houses that flooded in 2016 were not always repaired to the same standard. Some were gutted to the studs, dried properly and rebuilt with new wiring and insulation. Others got new drywall over framing that was never fully dried, or kept wiring and ductwork that sat underwater. We ask about flood history, look for water lines and staining in the attic and garage, check moisture behind baseboards, and open suspect walls early so remediation is priced before finishes.

commonIssues.title: Slab cracking and foundation movement
commonIssues.body: Baton Rouge's clay soils expand when wet and shrink during dry spells, and the parish sits across a known fault system that can crack slabs and streets along its trace. Older pier houses in Mid City and the Garden District drift out of level, while slab ranches in Broadmoor and Sherwood Forest show cracked tile, separated brick and sticking doors. A foundation evaluation before you finalize the offer tells you whether the movement is cosmetic, active or structural.

commonIssues.title: Under-slab plumbing failures
commonIssues.body: Mid-century ranches often have cast-iron drain lines under the slab that have cracked, scaled or settled, sometimes worsened by soil movement. Symptoms include slow drains, sewer smells and recurring backups. A camera inspection of the drain system is inexpensive compared with discovering a failed line after new flooring is installed. Where problems are found, we price repair or rerouting options so you can choose based on budget and hold period.

commonIssues.title: Attic ductwork and aging HVAC
commonIssues.body: In most Baton Rouge ranches, the air handler and ductwork sit in an attic that reaches extreme temperatures in summer. Old flex duct sags, leaks and grows mold at registers, and older systems struggle to dehumidify. Replacing or resealing ductwork alongside the HVAC equipment often makes a bigger difference in comfort and utility bills than equipment alone, and buyers and tenants notice when a house actually stays cool and dry.

commonIssues.title: Termites and wood rot
commonIssues.body: Subterranean termites, including Formosan colonies, are active in the Baton Rouge area. Older pier houses and any house with long-term leaks are especially vulnerable, and damage often hides in sills, door frames and wall bottoms. Humidity and heavy rain also cause wood rot in trim, fascia and siding. We recommend a wood-destroying insect inspection early and include treatment and framing repair in the scope when needed.

investorMarket:
Baton Rouge has several distinct investor markets inside one parish. The neighborhoods around LSU, including Southdowns, the Garden District edges and the apartment-heavy area near Tigerland, support strong demand from students, graduate students and university staff. Houses and small multifamily buildings there can rent well if they are durable and well managed, but they take hard use, so renovation choices matter.

Mid City, the Garden District and Capital Heights draw owner-occupant buyers who want older houses with character near downtown and the medical corridor. Flips there succeed when the structure, systems and flood history are addressed and the finishes suit the house. The mid-century ranch neighborhoods to the east and south, including Broadmoor, Sherwood Forest, Tara and Bernard Terrace, are the backbone of buy-and-hold investing, with simple floor plans that support repeatable rental renovations and BRRRR strategies.

North Baton Rouge, including Scotlandville near Southern University, has lower acquisition prices and many older houses in need of full renovation, along with more vacant and bank-owned inventory. Deals there require careful underwriting of repair costs and realistic rents. Suburban markets like Central, Zachary, Prairieville and Denham Springs have newer houses and strong school-driven demand, but flood history is a major question in many of them. Across all of these areas, our Pre-Offer Rehab Review is designed to put flood, foundation and systems risks next to your ARV before you commit capital.
permits:
Baton Rouge and East Baton Rouge Parish operate as a consolidated City-Parish government, and building permits are issued through the City-Parish Department of Development's permits and inspections division. Permits are generally required for structural work, roofing, electrical and plumbing changes, HVAC replacement, additions, window and door changes that alter openings, and conversions. Cosmetic work like paint, flooring and cabinet replacement usually does not require a permit unless walls or systems are opened.

Floodplain review is a major consideration. For houses in special flood hazard areas, extensive renovations can trigger substantial improvement requirements that force the house to meet current flood rules, and the parish strengthened its floodplain standards after 2016. Exterior changes in designated historic districts such as Spanish Town and Beauregard Town may need historic review before permits are issued.

Suburban cities, including Central, Zachary and Baker, have their own permit offices, and neighboring parishes such as Livingston and Ascension run separate processes. Louisiana requires contractors to be licensed or registered with the Louisiana State Licensing Board for Contractors, which is based in Baton Rouge, for residential and home improvement work above set thresholds. On every Baton Rouge job, Genstone lines up properly licensed trades, files the permits, books the inspections and gathers lien waivers before each draw is paid.
climate:
Baton Rouge has long, hot, humid summers, mild winters and heavy rainfall throughout the year. Intense rain events are the region's biggest weather risk, as 2016 showed, and they can flood areas well outside mapped flood zones. Hurricanes and tropical storms also reach the city; Gustav in 2008 and Ida in 2021 caused widespread wind damage and long power outages across the area.

For renovation work, that means drying in houses early during hurricane season, protecting materials from heavy rain, and making sure drainage around the house is part of the scope. Summer heat and humidity require air conditioning for proper installation of drywall, paint and flooring, and closed houses can grow mold quickly. Occasional hard freezes reach the area, and exposed pipes under raised houses or in exterior walls should be protected. Seasonal soil movement from wet and dry periods affects foundation repairs and finish work.

faqs.q: How do you check whether a Baton Rouge house flooded in 2016?
faqs.a: We ask the seller and agent directly, review disclosures, and look for physical evidence such as water lines in the garage or attic, replaced lower drywall, staining on framing, rusted electrical boxes and replaced ductwork. Moisture readings and opening suspect walls help confirm whether repairs were done properly. Flood zone and claim history matter too. We include our findings in the Pre-Offer Rehab Review so you can price any remaining remediation before you commit to the purchase.

faqs.q: Do you work in Central, Denham Springs and Prairieville?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone coordinates vetted, licensed local contractors across the Baton Rouge area, including Central, Zachary, Baker, Denham Springs, Walker, Prairieville, Gonzales and Port Allen. Each city or parish has its own permit office and floodplain rules, and your field manager handles permits in the correct jurisdiction. Many of these suburbs were affected by the 2016 flood, so flood history is part of every scope we write in those areas, not just in the city.

faqs.q: Are Baton Rouge rentals near LSU worth renovating?
faqs.a: They can be, but student rentals take hard use and turn over on a regular academic cycle, so durability and fast turns matter more than finish level. Waterproof flooring, washable walls, solid fixtures and reliable HVAC tend to pay off. Zoning and occupancy rules also affect how a house can be rented. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review evaluates repairs and helps you plan a renovation that suits the student and university rental market.

faqs.q: Do I need to be in Baton Rouge during the renovation?
faqs.a: No. A good share of our Baton Rouge clients live in other states. Your designated field manager coordinates local trades, handles City-Parish permits and inspections, and provides photos and milestone updates as work progresses. Draws are tied to completed work, nothing is paid upfront, and the final payment follows your approval of the finished house. You stay informed and involved in decisions without needing to travel to Louisiana for each stage.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Baton Rouge, LA | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Baton Rouge fix and flip rehab: flood-history checks, slab and pier repair, attic HVAC and finishes matched to Mid City, Garden District and suburban comps.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Baton Rouge
fix-flip.intro: Baton Rouge buyers and their agents have learned to ask one question before anything else: did this house flood? A flip that cannot answer clearly, with documentation, starts every showing on the defensive. After that, buyers and inspectors look at the slab or piers, the roof, the attic HVAC and the electrical panel. Genstone builds Baton Rouge flip scopes around those questions. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review checks flood history, foundation movement, systems and roof condition alongside your comps and ARV. The scope we write includes labor, materials and a draw schedule, often with more than one finish plan so you can compare costs against comps. A designated field manager coordinates licensed local trades, handles City-Parish permits and keeps the project moving to protect your margins.

sections.h2: Flood history is part of the product
sections.body:
In Baton Rouge, a renovated house is partly judged on what happened in 2016. If it flooded, buyers want to know how far the water rose, whether the house was gutted to the studs, whether the framing was dried and treated, and whether wiring, insulation and ductwork were replaced. If it did not flood, they want confidence that it did not.

We treat that history as part of the scope. During the Pre-Offer Rehab Review, we look for evidence of past water and incomplete repairs, and during demolition we open walls where questions remain. Where remediation is needed, it is done properly and documented with photos. Before listing, you can provide a summary of the work, permits and any flood-related repairs to the buyer's agent. Clear documentation does not change the facts of a house, but it often keeps a nervous buyer from walking away or asking for a large price reduction late in the process.

sections.h2: Slabs, piers and the systems inspectors check
sections.body:
After flood history, Baton Rouge inspectors focus on the foundation and major systems. On slab ranches in Broadmoor, Sherwood Forest and Tara, they look for cracked tile, separated brick, sticking doors and signs of under-slab plumbing problems. On older pier houses in Mid City and the Garden District, they check floor levels, pier condition and termite damage in sills and joists.

We evaluate those items first. A foundation specialist assesses movement and recommends repairs if needed. Drain lines are inspected with a camera. The attic HVAC system and ductwork are checked, since many older ranches have aging equipment and sagging, leaky flex duct that struggles in the summer heat. Electrical panels and wiring are reviewed for safety and insurability. Only after those items are addressed do we finalize the finish plan. That sequence produces a house that inspects well, supports the buyer's financing, and avoids callbacks from finish work damaged by unresolved foundation or plumbing problems.

Finish choices in Baton Rouge depend on the neighborhood and the buyer. In the Garden District, Mid City and Capital Heights, buyers appreciate original character such as hardwood floors, built-ins, period trim and porches, combined with updated kitchens and baths. In Southdowns and other areas near LSU, buyers include university staff and professionals who expect clean, modern updates in older houses.

In the ranch neighborhoods, buyers compare your flip with other renovated ranches and with newer suburban houses. Open kitchens where the structure allows, updated baths, durable flooring, fresh exterior paint and modern lighting tend to carry the sale. In the suburbs, including Central and Prairieville, buyers often compare against new construction, so finishes and systems need to feel complete. We can present more than one ARV plan in the scope so you can compare cost differences with what the comps support and choose the level that fits the house and neighborhood.

faqs.q: Can I flip a house in Baton Rouge that flooded in 2016?
faqs.a: Yes, many flooded houses have been renovated and resold successfully. The key is making sure remediation was done properly and documenting it. That may mean opening walls to confirm framing is dry and sound, replacing wiring, insulation and ductwork that were exposed to water, and providing buyers with clear records. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review looks for signs of incomplete repairs so you can price the work before buying.

faqs.q: What do Baton Rouge buyers' inspectors usually flag?
faqs.a: Common findings include slab or pier movement, cracked tile, sticking doors, under-slab drain problems, tired attic HVAC and sagging flex duct, older electrical panels, roof wear and termite damage. Evidence of past water intrusion is another frequent concern because of 2016. Addressing those items during the renovation and handing the buyer's agent a tidy file of permits and photos helps your Baton Rouge flip pass inspection and supports the buyer's financing and insurance.

faqs.q: Which Baton Rouge neighborhoods are best for flips?
faqs.a: It depends on your budget and buyer. The Garden District, Mid City, Capital Heights and Southdowns attract buyers who value older homes near downtown and LSU. Broadmoor, Sherwood Forest and Tara offer ranch houses with broad buyer appeal. Suburbs like Central and Prairieville draw buyers focused on schools. We help you compare repair costs with comps for the specific property during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Baton Rouge, LA | Genstone

brrrr.intro: Baton Rouge's mid-century ranch neighborhoods are well suited to BRRRR. Houses in Broadmoor, Sherwood Forest, Tara and Bernard Terrace have simple layouts, steady rental demand from workers in healthcare, government, education and the petrochemical industry, and a large supply of comparable sales once renovated. The risks are specific to the area: undocumented flood repairs, slab movement, under-slab plumbing and insurance costs that affect DSCR math. Genstone writes BRRRR scopes that address both the refinance and the long hold. We start with a free Pre-Offer Rehab Review that evaluates repairs, flood history and ARV before you commit. A designated field manager then coordinates licensed local trades and City-Parish permits. Genstone Financial offers DSCR rental loans if you want your refinance handled within the Genstone Companies.

sections.h2: What the Baton Rouge appraiser needs to see
sections.body:
Appraisers in Baton Rouge rely on nearby renovated sales, and in ranch neighborhoods there are often good comps to support a refinance. To be grouped with those comps, your house needs to show the same level of improvement: updated kitchen and bath, newer HVAC, sound roof, quality flooring and a house free of obvious foundation or moisture problems.

Flood history matters here too. If the house flooded in 2016, the appraiser or lender may ask how it was repaired, and a house with visible water damage or incomplete remediation can be marked down. Foundation cracks and sticking doors can raise similar concerns. We address those items during the renovation and keep documentation, including photos, permits and inspection results. At the end of the project, you receive a completed-work summary you can share with the appraiser. It does not determine value, but it helps the appraiser understand what was done and why the house belongs with renovated comps.

For a BRRRR refinance using a DSCR loan, the lender compares rent to expenses, including insurance. In Baton Rouge, flood insurance and homeowners coverage can vary widely depending on the property's flood zone, elevation, roof condition and history. A house in a special flood hazard area may require flood insurance that affects the DSCR ratio, and houses that flooded in 2016 outside those zones may still carry higher premiums or underwriting questions.

We help you assess those factors during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review, including flood zone and any available elevation information. In the renovation, items that commonly matter to insurers, such as roof condition, electrical systems and plumbing, are addressed and documented. A new roof, updated panel and repaired plumbing can make the house easier to insure. Insurance decisions belong to the carrier, so get quotes early, but a well-documented renovation gives you a better starting point for those conversations.

sections.h2: Durable finishes for long-term Baton Rouge rentals
sections.body:
After the refinance, the house needs to produce steady income with minimal maintenance. For Baton Rouge ranches, that starts with systems. A properly sized HVAC system with sealed, well-supported ductwork keeps tenants comfortable through long summers and reduces humidity problems. Repaired or replaced drain lines prevent backups, and updated electrical reduces safety risks.

Inside, we favor waterproof flooring throughout most of the house, washable paint in consistent colors, durable cabinets and counters, and fixtures that are easy to repair. Bathrooms need exhaust fans that vent outside to control moisture. Outside, gutters, downspouts and grading keep water away from the slab and reduce foundation movement. These choices increase upfront cost slightly but often reduce turnover expenses and maintenance calls over the hold period. Genstone Property Management can manage the property after the renovation if you want, and our one-year workmanship warranty covers the renovation itself, not tenant damage or normal wear.

faqs.q: Which Baton Rouge neighborhoods work best for BRRRR?
faqs.a: Mid-century ranch neighborhoods such as Broadmoor, Sherwood Forest, Tara and Bernard Terrace are common BRRRR targets because of their simple layouts, steady rental demand and supply of renovated comps. Areas closer to LSU can also work well for rentals. The best deals combine a reasonable purchase price, supportive comps and manageable insurance costs, which we help evaluate in the Pre-Offer Rehab Review.

faqs.q: Does 2016 flood history affect a Baton Rouge BRRRR refinance?
faqs.a: It can. Appraisers, lenders and insurers may ask about flood history and repairs. A house with incomplete remediation or visible damage may appraise lower or be harder to insure. Documenting proper repairs, including replaced wiring, insulation and ductwork where needed, helps answer those questions. We look for evidence of incomplete repairs before you buy and include remediation in the scope.

faqs.q: Can Genstone handle financing and management for my BRRRR?
faqs.a: Genstone Financial offers DSCR rental loans, fix-and-flip loans and lines of credit, and Genstone Property Management can lease and manage the property. Both are optional. If you use another lender or manager, we provide the scope, draw records and completion documentation they need. Your field manager focuses on completing the renovation so the house is ready for appraisal and tenants.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Baton Rouge | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Single-family rental renovation in Baton Rouge: durable ranch and bungalow rehabs, LSU-area rentals, fast documented turns and City-Parish permits handled.
rental-renovation.h1: Single-Family Rental Renovations in Baton Rouge
rental-renovation.intro: Baton Rouge rental portfolios tend to combine mid-century ranch houses in the eastern and southern neighborhoods with older bungalows near downtown and houses rented to students and staff near LSU. Each segment has different tenants and wear patterns, but they share local challenges: humid summers, attic HVAC systems working hard, slab and pier movement, and the possibility of flooding during heavy rain. Genstone renovates and turns single-family rentals for individual landlords, funds and institutional owners across the Baton Rouge area. We write a portfolio standard suited to local conditions, coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors, and handle City-Parish permits and inspections. A designated field manager documents each property. Genstone Field Services can also provide inspections, occupied maintenance and turn and make-ready work between larger renovations.

sections.h2: A rental standard for Baton Rouge houses
sections.body:
Our Baton Rouge rental standard focuses on durability, moisture control and consistent materials. Waterproof flooring is used in most rooms because it handles spills, pets and humidity. Walls are painted with washable finishes in consistent colors to simplify touch-ups. Cabinets, counters and fixtures are chosen for durability and easy repair, with parts available from local suppliers.

Systems receive particular attention. HVAC equipment must be properly sized, and attic ductwork should be sealed, insulated and supported, because leaky ducts in a hot attic reduce efficiency and can cause condensation problems. Water heaters, plumbing fixtures and drain lines are checked or replaced as needed. Older pier houses get vapor barriers and checks for termite damage, while slab ranches are evaluated for under-slab plumbing problems. Every house receives working smoke and carbon monoxide detectors, GFCI protection where required and secure doors and windows. A consistent standard reduces maintenance costs and simplifies future renovations and turns.

sections.h2: Renting near LSU and Southern University
sections.body:
Rentals near LSU, including Southdowns, the Garden District edges and the blocks around Tigerland, serve undergraduates, graduate students and university staff. Houses near Southern University in Scotlandville serve a similar market on the north side. These tenants provide steady demand, but they tend to turn over on an academic schedule and can be hard on a house.

For these properties, durability matters more than high-end finishes. We favor waterproof flooring, scrubbable paint, solid-core doors and commercial-grade hardware, durable counters, and bathroom fans that actually clear steam from the room. Reliable HVAC is essential when a group of roommates is home all summer. Exterior lighting and good locks improve safety. Because move-outs cluster around the start and end of terms, we plan turns in advance so houses are ready when demand peaks in late summer. Occupancy rules can limit how many unrelated tenants share a house, so confirm the rules for the specific property before planning bedroom counts.

Every turn is an opportunity to check for problems that can become expensive in Baton Rouge. After a tenant moves out, a field inspection documents the condition of the house with photos and creates a scope based on your standard. Tenant damage is separated from normal wear so security deposit decisions are clear.

We also check for signs of moisture intrusion, foundation movement and termite activity. Heavy rain events can bring water into houses that have never flooded before, and early signs like damp baseboards, musty odors or stained drywall should be investigated. Cracks, sticking doors and uneven floors can indicate foundation movement. Mud tubes or damaged wood may point to termites. Trades are scheduled in sequence so repairs, paint and flooring happen efficiently. You approve the scope, follow progress remotely and pay for completed work. Completion records provide a baseline for the next lease and documentation for any insurance or tenant questions.

faqs.q: Do you manage rental turns in Baton Rouge?
faqs.a: Yes. Our Baton Rouge work covers both full rental renovations and the recurring turns between tenants, and Genstone Field Services adds make-ready, inspections and occupied maintenance for owners who want ongoing coverage. Each turn begins with a photo-documented inspection and a scope written to your portfolio standard. You approve it, watch progress remotely and pay only for completed work, which keeps vacancy short without paying ahead of the crews.

faqs.q: What should a Baton Rouge rental renovation include?
faqs.a: Most Baton Rouge rental scopes should cover HVAC and attic ductwork, drain lines under the slab, electrical safety, roof condition, foundation movement, moisture and termite risk, and durable interior finishes. Pre-1978 houses require lead-safe work practices when painted surfaces are disturbed. We price every line on its own so you can choose what to fix now and what to schedule for the next turn or budget year.

faqs.q: Can you work on rentals across East Baton Rouge Parish and nearby parishes?
faqs.a: Yes. We coordinate vetted, licensed local contractors in Baton Rouge and the surrounding communities, including Central, Zachary, Baker, Denham Springs, Prairieville and Gonzales. Livingston and Ascension parishes run their own permits and floodplain rules separate from the City-Parish, and your field manager handles each one. A single portfolio standard keeps materials and quality consistent no matter which side of the Amite River a house sits on.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex & 2–4 Unit Renovation in Baton Rouge | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Baton Rouge duplex and fourplex renovations near LSU, Mid City and Old South Baton Rouge: shared systems, phased occupied work and permits handled.
multifamily-renovation.h1: Duplex and Small Multifamily Renovation in Baton Rouge
multifamily-renovation.intro: Baton Rouge's small multifamily buildings are concentrated in a few areas. Near LSU, you find duplexes, triplexes and fourplexes built for student and university renters, many from the 1960s through the 1980s. Mid City and Old South Baton Rouge have older duplexes and houses divided into apartments, while scattered brick fourplexes appear along older commercial corridors. These buildings can produce strong rental income, but they share roofs, foundations, sewer lines and sometimes electrical services, so problems affect several tenants at once. Genstone renovates 2–4 unit buildings for investors seeking higher rents, lower operating costs or a value-add refinance. We plan work around occupied units, coordinate vetted, licensed local trades, and handle City-Parish permits and inspections. A designated field manager keeps the work documented from start to finish.

sections.body:
Many small multifamily buildings near LSU were built for students and have experienced decades of heavy use. Common issues include worn flooring, damaged doors and hardware, aging HVAC units, older electrical panels and plumbing that has been repaired many times. Some buildings have been altered over the years, with unpermitted bedrooms or layout changes.

Renovating these buildings starts with confirming the legal unit count and any occupancy limits that apply. We then evaluate shared systems, including the roof, foundation, sewer line and electrical service, before planning unit interiors. Inside, we focus on durable, repeatable materials: waterproof flooring, washable paint, solid doors and hardware, durable counters and fixtures that are easy to repair. HVAC systems are sized and installed to handle Baton Rouge humidity. Exterior lighting, secure entries and fire safety features are also important. These choices help reduce maintenance and turnover costs in a market where units turn over regularly.

sections.h2: Older conversions in Mid City and Old South Baton Rouge
sections.body:
Older houses divided into apartments in Mid City and Old South Baton Rouge can have real character and steady rental demand from downtown and hospital workers, but they often hide problems. Layouts may be irregular, plumbing and electrical may have been extended piece by piece, and fire separation between units may be incomplete or missing. Pier foundations in these neighborhoods often sit out of level, and termite damage is common in sills and framing near old leaks.

Before planning finishes, we confirm the legal unit count with the City-Parish, map which systems are shared and evaluate the structure. Work may include releveling or pier repair, separating utilities, upgrading the electrical service, adding smoke and carbon monoxide detection and improving separation between units. Buildings near Spanish Town and Beauregard Town may also fall inside historic districts where exterior changes need review. We list each building-level item separately so you can compare costs with expected rents and decide what to address now and what can wait for unit turnover.

sections.h2: Phasing work around Baton Rouge tenants
sections.body:
Most small multifamily acquisitions in Baton Rouge come with tenants in at least some units. We phase work so vacant units get full renovations first, while occupied units are handled at lease turnover or during agreed access windows. Exterior work, including roofing, siding, gutters, painting and drainage correction, can proceed without entering anyone's home.

Shared-system work, such as a sewer lateral replacement or an electrical service upgrade, is scheduled with advance notice and the shortest practical shutoff. Losing air conditioning in a Baton Rouge August is more than an inconvenience, so HVAC work in occupied units is planned to finish within the day wherever possible. In buildings constructed before 1978, lead-safe practices and containment protect families in adjacent units. Near LSU, many leases follow the academic calendar, which creates a natural renovation window each summer when several units empty at once. Your field manager coordinates schedules with you or your property manager so tenants are informed and crews work in a sensible order.

faqs.q: Can you renovate a Baton Rouge fourplex while tenants live there?
faqs.a: Usually. Vacant units are renovated first, and occupied units are handled at turnover or during scheduled access windows. Exterior work and anything touching shared plumbing or electrical is announced ahead of time with brief, planned shutoffs. Air conditioning replacements are timed so tenants are not without cooling through a hot night. Your field manager keeps you or your property manager updated on each phase of the Baton Rouge project.

faqs.q: What should I check before buying a duplex near LSU?
faqs.a: Confirm the legal unit count and any occupancy limits, then evaluate the roof, foundation, sewer line, electrical service, HVAC units and fire safety features. Student buildings often show heavy wear and signs of unpermitted bedroom additions, so look closely at layouts. Our Pre-Offer Rehab Review evaluates these items and estimates repair costs so you can compare them with realistic rents for the LSU market before making an offer.

faqs.q: Do you renovate older converted houses in Baton Rouge?
faqs.a: Yes. Converted older houses in Mid City, Old South Baton Rouge and the neighborhoods around downtown frequently need pier or foundation work, electrical upgrades, utility separation and better fire separation between units. We evaluate those items before talking about finishes and list each one separately in the scope, so you can decide what to do right away and what can follow as units turn over.

fha-203k.intro: Baton Rouge has a large supply of houses that are affordable to first-time buyers but need significant work before they meet FHA standards. Mid-century ranches may need a roof, HVAC, plumbing and electrical updates, while older bungalows may need foundation repairs and termite work. An FHA 203(k) loan lets an owner-occupant buyer finance the purchase and renovation in one mortgage. Genstone Construction is an FHA 203(k) Certified Contractor, working with buyers, agents, lenders and consultants across the Baton Rouge area. We prepare detailed bids that fit the program and the property, flag flood history or foundation issues early, and help everyone understand the scope before closing. After closing, a designated field manager coordinates vetted, licensed local trades, handles City-Parish permits and documents each draw.

sections.h2: Choosing Limited or Standard in Baton Rouge
sections.body:
The Limited 203(k) handles non-structural repairs, with a cap of $75,000. It can work well for a Broadmoor, Sherwood Forest or Tara ranch that needs a new roof, HVAC and ductwork, plumbing and electrical updates, flooring and kitchen or bath improvements. Many mid-century Baton Rouge houses fit this profile.

The Standard 203(k) is required for structural repairs, such as foundation work, major termite damage, room additions or significant layout changes. It requires a HUD-approved 203(k) consultant, and repairs need to total at least $5,000 under the program. Older pier houses in Mid City and the Garden District often need a Standard 203(k) if releveling or framing repair is required. We help buyers and agents determine which option fits during the initial walk-through, because discovering structural issues after the contract is signed can delay closing and require a new bid. Flood history should also be reviewed early, since past water damage can affect the scope.

sections.h2: Baton Rouge houses that fit the program
sections.body:
Good 203(k) candidates in Baton Rouge usually have a sound structure and clear, fixable problems. A brick ranch with an aging roof, original electrical panel, old HVAC and dated kitchen is a common example. Older bungalows near downtown and LSU can also be strong candidates for buyers who want character and are willing to take on foundation or termite repairs through a Standard 203(k).

More difficult properties include houses with extensive flood damage that was never properly repaired, unresolved structural issues, or significant unpermitted work. Houses in special flood hazard areas may face substantial improvement limits on how much work can be done without meeting current flood rules. These issues do not always rule out a 203(k), but they require careful evaluation before the buyer commits. Lead paint rules apply to houses built before 1978, which includes many of the city's older neighborhoods, and they affect how painted surfaces are handled during renovation.

A 203(k) bid must work for the lender, the consultant on Standard loans and the buyer. Our bids break out labor and materials by trade, describe each repair clearly and include a draw schedule tied to completed work. On Standard loans, we coordinate with the consultant to make sure our bid matches the work write-up before submission.

Once the loan closes, the Baton Rouge renovation moves in a set order. Structural repairs typically come first, followed by HVAC, plumbing and electrical, and then finishes. Each draw request includes photos and completion documentation, and the lender or consultant inspects the work before releasing funds. Your field manager schedules City-Parish permits and inspections so approvals are in place for each draw. The buyer is never asked for money before work begins, and the last payment is released only after the house is complete and approved. Agents and lenders receive regular updates so they can keep the buyer informed, and the buyer can see photos of the house at each stage.

faqs.q: Can a 203(k) loan cover HVAC and ductwork in Baton Rouge?
faqs.a: Yes. Replacing HVAC equipment and ductwork is a common 203(k) repair and is usually eligible under the Limited 203(k) if no structural work is required. In Baton Rouge, replacing old attic flex duct along with the equipment often improves comfort, humidity control and power bills noticeably. We include equipment and ductwork details in the bid so the lender and appraiser can see exactly what is being installed.

faqs.q: Can I use a 203(k) on a house that flooded in 2016?
faqs.a: Possibly. It depends on how the house was repaired after the water and its current condition. If remediation was incomplete, more work may be needed, such as replacing wiring or insulation that stayed in the walls. Houses in flood hazard areas may also face substantial improvement limits. We evaluate flood history and remaining damage before the buyer commits, so the loan type and scope are realistic from the start.

faqs.q: Is Genstone certified for FHA 203(k) work in Baton Rouge?
faqs.a: Yes, Genstone is a certified FHA 203(k) contractor, and we take on projects throughout the Baton Rouge area. We prepare bids for lenders and consultants, coordinate vetted, licensed local trades and document each draw. The lender makes final decisions on the loan and the contractor, so check with your loan officer early and bring us in as soon as you have a target house.

reo-renovation.title: REO & Bank-Owned Renovation in Baton Rouge | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: Baton Rouge REO renovation for servicers, banks and GSEs: flood and mold damage, theft, termites and code issues on vacant houses stabilized and documented.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovation in Baton Rouge
reo-renovation.intro: Bank-owned houses in Baton Rouge often come with layered problems. Some were damaged in the 2016 flood and never fully repaired before the owner fell behind. Others sat closed through humid summers and developed mold, or lost HVAC equipment and copper to theft. Roof leaks invite termites, and overgrown yards can draw code enforcement. Genstone works with mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and Government-Sponsored Enterprises, for which we are a preferred contractor, to secure, stabilize and renovate REO properties across East Baton Rouge Parish and nearby parishes. Preservation, inspections and code compliance run through Genstone Field Services, and the renovation team scopes and completes repairs using vetted, licensed contractors from the Baton Rouge area. Every step is documented for asset managers and investor reporting.

sections.body:
The first step on a Baton Rouge REO is to understand and stop the damage. Our initial inspection documents the property with photos and a written report, identifying immediate hazards, active leaks, mold, termite activity, foundation movement, theft of HVAC equipment or copper and signs of unauthorized entry. We also look for evidence of 2016 flood damage that was covered rather than corrected, such as new drywall over stained studs or original wiring left in walls that sat underwater.

Stabilization often includes securing doors and windows, tarping or temporarily repairing roof leaks, drying wet areas, removing debris and addressing mold growth. Where utilities are available, running HVAC or dehumidifiers can slow mold growth in humid months. Emergency items are separated from the full repair list so asset managers can approve urgent work quickly. Documentation from this stage supports insurance claims for damage that occurred during the holding period and gives asset managers a clear basis for deciding whether to sell as-is or invest in repairs before listing.

Vacant houses in Baton Rouge can draw code enforcement attention quickly once grass grows tall in the long growing season, debris piles up, windows are broken or roofs are damaged. Open cases can lead to fines, liens or parish-ordered cleanup billed back to the owner. Genstone Field Services handles the preservation work that keeps properties compliant, including securing, boarding, debris removal, lawn care, winterization where needed and recurring inspections.

When notices are issued, we track them, complete the required work, document it with photos and coordinate reinspection. If permitted work is needed to resolve a violation, such as roof replacement or structural repair, our field manager pulls permits through the City-Parish and schedules inspections. North Baton Rouge and Scotlandville carry more long-vacant inventory than other parts of the parish, and those houses often need more stabilization before an accurate repair scope is possible. For properties in special flood hazard areas, we consider floodplain rules before recommending major repairs. Ongoing preservation reduces the chance of new violations and protects value while the property is held or marketed.

Asset managers need repair options that match their disposition plan. For Baton Rouge REO properties, we typically price several levels of work: safety, code and weatherproofing items only; a market-ready scope addressing what buyers' lenders and insurers commonly flag, such as roof condition, electrical systems and HVAC; and, where the numbers support it, a fuller renovation for owner-occupant buyers in neighborhoods like Broadmoor, Sherwood Forest or the Garden District.

Each option includes labor, materials, debris removal and dumpsters and is organized by priority: safety and code compliance, weatherproofing, structure and systems, then cosmetic work. Every completed task is documented with photos, and lien waivers and contractor compliance paperwork are collected with each payment. If a buyer's inspection identifies additional issues, the same field manager can price and complete repairs without restarting the vendor process. That continuity helps servicers, GSE programs and institutional owners keep organized files and move East Baton Rouge Parish properties toward closing with fewer surprises.

faqs.q: What damage is common in vacant Baton Rouge houses?
faqs.a: Mold from humidity and leaks, roof damage, termite activity, foundation movement, stolen HVAC equipment and copper, and incomplete repairs from the 2016 flood are the conditions we see most. Our first inspection documents each condition and separates emergency items from the full repair list so asset managers can approve urgent work quickly. In summer months, fast approval on leaks and drying keeps mold from spreading into a much larger remediation.

faqs.q: Can you handle code violations on Baton Rouge REO properties?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone Field Services can complete cleanup, securing, lawn care and the other preservation work needed to answer code notices, document it with photos and coordinate reinspection. When a violation calls for permitted repairs, our field manager pulls them through the City-Parish and schedules inspections so the case can be closed out. Recurring lawn and debris service then helps keep the property from drawing a new notice.

faqs.q: Do you work with servicers and GSEs in Baton Rouge?
faqs.a: We do. Asset managers at servicers, banks, REITs and funds use Genstone for Baton Rouge files, and the company is a preferred contractor for Government-Sponsored Enterprises. Each file gets photos, condition reports, priced repair options, lien waivers and completion records, so reviewers can follow what was found, what was approved and what was finished. Field Services covers preservation and code compliance alongside the renovation team.
